problem_statement: A caller that converts an LwM2M Float TLV value into the fixpoint representation (the conversion exercised by the unit tests) produces wrong or unacceptable results for several inputs, and accepts inputs it should reject. A Float value whose magnitude is large enough to exceed the fixpoint integer's range returns a wrong (overflowing) number instead of the largest representable value, and a value whose magnitude is so small that it falls below the format's resolution returns a wrong number instead of zero. The reserved encodings for infinity and for NaN are accepted and return a usable number instead of being rejected. An eight-byte Float value (binary64) is not decoded at all: it is read as a four-byte value and comes back as a plausible but wrong number (for example, 1.0 is returned as 1.875) with no error, so a legal eight-byte value yields an incorrect result. A Float TLV whose length is neither four nor eight bytes (for example 5, 6, 7, or more than 8) is accepted and decoded instead of being rejected, even though the LwM2M specification allows only the two widths. Required behavior: values that fit the fixpoint range are converted correctly; a finite value outside the representable range yields the extreme representable value; a value below the resolution yields zero; infinity and NaN are rejected; an eight-byte value is decoded as binary64 and agrees with the same number encoded as binary32; and any length other than exactly four or eight bytes is rejected with no value produced.

superseded_statements.problem_statement: lwm2m_tlv_float32_to_fix() takes its shift count from the exponent byte of a received Float TLV, so a packet can drive the shift past the width of int32_t (undefined behavior, with left-shift overflow); the two reserved exponents (infinity/NaN and zero/subnormals) went through the same shift; a binary64 (8-byte) value was decoded as binary32 (returning a plausible wrong number, e.g. 1.0 as 1.875, with no error); and any length other than exactly 4 or 8 was accepted and decoded from its first four bytes. The fix adds a saturating significand_to_fix, rejects infinity/NaN (returns 0), returns 0 for zero/subnormals, decodes both binary32 and binary64 widths, and rejects any length that is neither 4 nor 8.
check_issues: `problem_statement` names code of the fix that the tests do not use (significand_to_fix); describe what a caller observes instead

causal_chain: The test builds raw IEEE 754 encodings and drives the conversion directly. For the binary32 cases it sets the TLV length to 4 and asserts the returned size is 4 and the converted fixpoint value matches the expected value (or that a rejected input returns size 0 and value 0). Under the unfixed conversion the large-magnitude and tiny-magnitude values yield an overflowing or wrong value instead of the saturating extreme or zero, and the infinity/NaN encodings are accepted, so those assertions fail. For the binary64 cases it sets the length to 8 and expects an 8-byte result; the unfixed conversion reads the value as a four-byte binary32 regardless of length, returning a different number and size 4, so the asserted size and value do not match. For the scales cases the same conversion is exercised at other fixpoint scales, where the out-of-range and edge values again yield wrong results. For the both-widths-agree case it decodes the same number at four and eight bytes and asserts the two results are equal; because the eight-byte input is decoded as binary32 it produces a different number, so the equality assertion fails. For the malformed-length case it loops over every length from 0 to 16 except 4 and 8 and asserts each is rejected (size 0, value 0); the unfixed conversion accepts those lengths and decodes the first four bytes, producing a nonzero value and a nonzero size, so the assertion fails.
